Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

issues.explanation: The trigger set is mostly coherent with rape trauma (locked/confined spaces, sexual-violence comments), but sirens are hard to connect to the rest of this profile and trauma context. With strong Negative Appraisals↔Threat and links from both to Triggers, the triggers should plausibly cue the patient's threat meanings; sirens do not fit the sexual-assault/confinement theme represented by the other trigger and appraisal items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilant unsafe-world items (back to wall, staying alert to sleep) fit well, but 'taking too many risks' pulls in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile with the same immediate threat style. It also lacks support elsewhere in the profile, since no other items suggest disinhibition, anger, numbing, or self-destructive coping.

vignette:
Kwame's Story

Kwame was thirty-seven when the attack happened, though he would later mark his life in two distinct eras: before and after a single night in March. He had been at a professional conference in Atlanta, staying in a hotel near the airport, when a man he'd met at the bar-someone who seemed friendly, who had talked about psychology and trauma work-had invited him back to his room. Kwame had gone willingly. He had trusted the conversation, the sense of intellectual kinship. What followed was a violent assault in a locked hotel room, the man's weight pinning him to the bed, his own voice seeming to come from someone else's body as he begged for it to stop. The lock on the door had made escape impossible. The windows looked out onto a parking lot where no one could hear him. When it was over, Kwame had lain there in the dark, feeling the weight of the man's presence even after he'd left the room, and had understood in that moment something that would reshape every day that followed: he was not safe anywhere.

For weeks afterward, Kwame had tried to function. He'd returned to his practice, seeing clients in his office in Durham, a space he'd always found professional and calm. But something had fractured. Within a month, he'd rearranged his entire office so that his desk faced the door and he could see into the waiting room. He'd begun positioning himself with his back against the wall during sessions, a habit so pronounced that one client had asked if he was uncomfortable. He wasn't sleeping well either-his mind wouldn't quiet at night, and he'd lie awake convinced that vigilance was the only thing keeping him alive. The belief that he was fundamentally exposed, that the trauma was written across his face for anyone to read, had begun to calcify. He was certain that his clients could see what had happened to him, that they would sense his weakness, his failure to protect himself. When a female client had mentioned her own experience of assault in passing, Kwame had felt the room tilt. The conversation about sexual violence, innocent as it was, had triggered a cascade of panic-his heart racing, his hands trembling-and he'd had to excuse himself to the bathroom.

The triggers began to multiply in ways that seemed to follow a logic he couldn't quite name. Locked spaces became intolerable. When a client's session ran late and Kwame found himself in his office with the door closed, he would feel his chest tighten, an urgent need to leave that he could barely suppress. But what frightened him most was the presence of men. Being alone with a male colleague, even briefly, sent his nervous system into overdrive. He'd started avoiding meetings that were one-on-one, scheduling consultations only in group settings, making excuses. His supervisor had noticed-had asked if everything was all right-but Kwame couldn't articulate it. How could he explain that the simple fact of a man's presence in an enclosed space had become a threat that his body registered before his mind could reason it away?

What Kwame had come to believe, in the months that followed, was that he had no control over what happened to him, that his future was a foregone conclusion of further harm. He couldn't stop bad things from happening. This conviction didn't sit separately from his vigilance; it fed it. His inability to relax, even in his own apartment with the door locked and the lights on, was rooted in the conviction that relaxation was a luxury he couldn't afford, that the moment he let his guard down was the moment danger would find him. The hypervigilance-the need to position himself so he could see the room, the inability to fall asleep without first checking the locks-became the logical response to a world that had already proven itself catastrophic. And this constant state of threat monitoring, this exhausting surveillance of his environment and of other people's intentions, only deepened his sense of hopelessness. He was trapped in a loop where his fear confirmed his belief that the world was dangerous, and his belief that he was helpless made the fear feel justified.

By the time Kwama called for an appointment, six months had passed. He was thinner, his eyes hollow with sleep deprivation. He'd begun considering whether he could continue practicing as a psychologist-how could he help others when he couldn't help himself? That question, more than any other, had finally pushed him to seek help. He sat in the intake room with his back to the corner, and when asked what had brought him in, he said simply: "I'm drowning, and I don't know how to stop."
